newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Battered Swiss use Churchill ads to polish image. [CORRECTED 13:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Battered Swiss use Churchill ads to polish image. [CORRECTED 13:00 GMT]

text.p: A pillar of the Swiss business establishment on Friday cited Winston Churchill's wartime praise of Switzerland in an international ad campaign to polish the country's image amid accusations it cosied up to the Nazis.

Winterthur Schweizerische Versicherungs-Gesellschaft, the country's second-biggest insurer, put a full-page advertisement in the Financial Times reminding the paper's global audience of the former British prime minister's defence of the Swiss.

It was the boldest stroke yet by Swiss business, which generally acknowledges it badly underestimated the flak it would face over charges that secretive Swiss banks and other firms dealt extensively with the Nazis and then later covered it up.

"Of all the neutrals Switzerland has the greatest right to distinction," the 50,000 Swiss franc Churchill ad trumpets, quoting comments he made in December 1944 (corrects year from 1994) as the tide of war had turned against Hitler.
"What does it matter whether she has been able to give us the commercial advantages we desire or has given too many to the Germans, to keep herself alive?
"She has been a democratic state, standing for freedom in self-defence among her mountains, and in thought, in spite of race, largely on our side."
"Switzerland", "democratic state" and "on our side" stand out in bold type.

Winterthur spokeswoman Anna-Marie Kappeler said the ad was a one-off event that followed similar ads in two Swiss newspapers on Thursday. It capped events Winterthur sponsored to mark Churchill's famous "let Europe arise" speech in Zurich in 1946.

But it also offered the chance to buff Switzerland's image amid widespread satisfaction abroad that the smug Swiss had come under fire from Jewish organisations, prominent foreign politicians and the press, especially in Britain.
"It is certainly a reaction to the attacks that have arisen, not in the sense that we have anything to hide...but one cannot see this in such a one-sided way," Kappeler said.

"This is also a mouthpiece for many Swiss who say: 'Not everything was wrong. We were in an extreme situation, under pressure, a small country'...This was the message and many people were waiting for it," she added.

Swiss officials reacted with relative nonchalance at first to accusations that Switzerland misled the Allies about how much gold it had bought from Nazi Germany, which used gold looted from conquered lands and peoples to finance its war effort.
Swiss business leaders still play down the potential impact the furore could have on Switzerland as a financial centre, but it is clear many executives are watching events with concern.
"This can hurt us, of course. You will have to ask the bankers how they see it but I think we have to take this very seriously. This is a very touchy question," Kappeler said.
The Churchill ad was the brainchild of Winterthur president Peter Spaelti, a former member of parliament.
"He said we had to do something positive to restore confidence," said his aide, Roger Schaerer.

"As a leading Swiss insurance company we had nothing to do with the Nazis -- and our internal records show we opposed the Nazis -- so would could do this. If a bank that perhaps was involved had done it, it would have been wrong," he added.
Praise for the ad has flooded in from newspaper readers, politicians and others eager to see Switzerland's reputation restored. But the flap has left even Swiss commentators hurt.

"Where are our friends? They should spring to our side," Sonntagsblick columnist Frank A. Meyer wrote this week. "Did we ever have friends? We only ever had friendly business partners, because it was good to do busines with us. But friends?"
"We are very alone."
